entities.summary:
Bertold von Henneberg-Römhild (1442–1504), a pivotal figure in late medieval German politics and ecclesiastical reform, served as Archbishop-Elector of Mainz from 1484 and imperial chancellor from 1486. His career unfolded during a critical juncture for the Holy Roman Empire, a period marked by attempts to centralize imperial authority and reform its fragmented constitutional structure. As a leading proponent of imperial reform, he championed initiatives aimed at establishing a more cohesive legal and administrative framework, contending with the complex interplay of princely power, papal influence, and nascent national identity across Central Europe, especially in the wake of growing Ottoman threats.

Elevated to the powerful see of Mainz in 1484, Bertold quickly became the intellectual and political architect of the "Reichsreform" movement. His most significant achievement was his instrumental role in the Diet of Worms in 1495, where he successfully advocated for the establishment of the *Reichskammergericht* (Imperial Chamber Court) and the *Ewiger Landfriede* (Perpetual Public Peace), which outlawed private feuds. He also pushed for the creation of the *Reichsregiment* (Imperial Government) in 1500, an attempt to create a standing executive body, though this institution proved short-lived due to resistance from Emperor Maximilian I and various princes. Bertold's vision encompassed a stronger, more unified Empire, capable of effective governance and defense against external threats and internal disorder.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Bertold von Henneberg-Römhild was a principal architect of the *Reichsreform* movement, establishing the *Reichskammergericht* and *Ewiger Landfriede* which fundamentally reshaped the legal and political landscape of the Holy Roman Empire for centuries. His efforts significantly contributed to the Empire's constitutional development, influencing governance until its dissolution in 1806.
